title: Take Your Time
idea: Tap-to-pay made buying things faster and the day quieter. For many people, the chat at the till was the only conversation they had. Mastercard owns that, and gives a minute back. Small merchants display a simple 'Take Your Time' sign and can switch on a gentler, slower payment sound. Any customer can pause their tap, and the person behind the counter answers with a real conversation. No one has to say they're lonely, and no data is used. Participating shops get free signage and fee relief, and become neighbourhood hubs for regulars. Priceless becomes something small and human: a minute of someone's time. The campaign starts with a pilot in a few neighbourhoods, grows through the stories of shopkeepers and regulars, and ends with a simple line: the fastest way to pay shouldn't be the end of the conversation.
follow_up_questions: What other everyday, frictionless moments (deliveries, ride-hailing, self-checkout) have quietly removed human contact, and could a brand give them back? | How could the slower sound or signal be designed so it feels warm and recognisable without becoming a cliché or a burden on staff? | How would you measure success in a way that respects privacy and avoids turning loneliness into a metric, such as merchant stories, repeat visits or something else?

title: The Second Fitting
idea: At Dior, a first fitting makes a piece yours. A second fitting makes it last. We invite owners to bring back a treasured piece (a mother's jacket, a well-loved Lady Dior) to the atelier to be restored, reshaped or reborn. Each time, the artisans stitch a discreet Fitting Number inside the lining, a signed record of another life lived. Short films follow the garments and the hands that renew them, and an exhibition celebrates the most-fitted pieces as the most precious. When a piece moves on, its lineage travels with it through a Dior-certified Next Owner programme. Repair stops being an afterthought and becomes the highest form of luxury: proof that something was made to be kept.
follow_up_questions: What would make a visible sign of repair feel like a status symbol rather than a flaw, and how might other categories borrow that logic? | Which moments in a Dior piece's life (inheritance, weight change, a new job, a milestone) are the most emotionally powerful occasions to invite someone back to the atelier? | How could the same lineage idea be extended to people who do not yet own Dior, so that they can experience care and craft without buying a full-price new piece?

title: Missed You
idea: Tapping to pay has made life quicker and quieter. For many people, the barista who knows their order is the only person they speak to all day. 'Missed You' turns that routine into a quiet safety net. Customers opt in and choose a few local places. If their usual visit pattern pauses for a time they set, the shop gets an anonymous nudge: 'One of your regulars hasn't been in.' No spending data, no name, just a prompt to be human: save the usual table, write a note, ask 'where have you been?' Customers can also pick one person to be gently alerted. The campaign tells real regular-and-shopkeeper stories, and shows that money can't buy being missed, but a payment can be the thing that notices you're gone. Priceless, rebuilt around attention.
follow_up_questions: What is the smallest, most dignified gesture a merchant could make that feels like warmth rather than surveillance or charity? | How could the idea reach people who would never opt in themselves, for example through family, neighbours, charities or city partners? | Beyond payments, what other everyday systems quietly remove human contact, and could a brand reverse that in a similar way?

title: Paid Before You Were Ready
idea: Nobody pays the amateur, yet you can't feel professional until someone pays you. For freelancers and side-hustlers, the first paycheck starts with a document you design yourself. Canva steps into that gap with a First Invoice Kit and a new ritual: the PAID stamp. When your first invoice is settled, you stamp it in Canva and share it, with the amount hidden by default. The stamp becomes a badge of 'I'm a professional now', a shareable sticker and a community wall of first PAIDs. Creators show the invoice they sent while still doubting themselves, then the stamp. Canva becomes the tool behind the moment you become a pro, not only a tool for making posts.
follow_up_questions: What other 'proof of professionalism' moments (a first business card, a first pitch, a first client email) could the stamp ritual extend to? | How could the PAID stamp work as a physical or cultural object, such as a real rubber stamp, a bell or a desk trophy, so it travels beyond screens? | Which partners (payment platforms, freelance marketplaces, coworking spaces, creator communities) could make the first-PAID moment more meaningful without Canva claiming to handle payments?

title: The First Thing I Got Paid For
idea: Your first paycheck doesn't just pay for your time. It pays for the first thing you made that you had no idea how to make. Canva turns that moment into a campaign: young workers share the first piece of work they were paid for, a deck, a flyer, a proposal, beside a blurred paycheck. Each story shows the 'nobody taught me this' panic and the quiet pride after. Canva makes every piece remixable as a template, so the next new hire can start from someone else's first. A Day One pack helps managers support new starters, linking the emotion to workplace use. The tone is warm, funny and proud, never financial advice.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job tasks are the most universal and the most cringe-worthy, and could they become a recurring story format? | How could employers and managers join the campaign without making it feel like corporate onboarding? | What would make someone proud, rather than embarrassed, to publicly share the rough first version of their work?

title: The Slow Lane
idea: Tap-to-pay made paying silent. For many people who live alone, the checkout was the last daily conversation. The Slow Lane is Mastercard's counter-move: a Priceless programme that turns neighbourhood businesses into places where lingering is welcome. Cafés, barbers and corner shops opt in with a simple kit: a 'No rush' counter, a terminal that says 'Stay a while?' after the tap, and a slowed-down Mastercard tap sound that works like an audible pause. Participating spots appear on a map, and nobody is ever labelled lonely; the invitation is simply 'no rush'. Films celebrate unhurried five-minute exchanges, and the call to action is 'Be a regular somewhere.' Success is measured in repeat visits and merchant stories, not checkout speed: the fastest network in the world choosing, once, to be slower on purpose.
follow_up_questions: What other moments in the payment journey (the tap, the receipt, the tip, the delivery handover) could be redesigned to invite a human connection rather than remove it? | How could the campaign help people accept an invitation to connect without having to admit they are lonely, and which cultural cues of belonging (regulars, rituals, nicknames) might work in different markets? | Who are the most credible partners (local councils, loneliness charities, independent merchants, community figures) to co-own The Slow Lane so it feels like a shared movement and not a brand stunt?

title: First Paid
idea: Nobody remembers the exact amount of their first paycheck. Everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the pitch deck, the wedding invitation, the logo for a friend's startup. First Paid turns that memory into a shareable 'receipt': a Canva template that pairs the work that earned your first money with the date, who paid you, and a blurred amount. Anyone can add what it meant to them. We seed a public gallery with creators, freelancers and small business owners, and show the receipts as framed pay stubs on posters and feeds. Employers can use a team version to celebrate a new hire's first paid project. The campaign celebrates the start of careers and quietly proves that much of it began in Canva.
follow_up_questions: What is the most surprising or humble 'first paid thing' you or someone you know made, and what would it say about how careers really start? | How might the 'First Paid' receipt change across cultures where the first paycheck goes to parents or family rather than to the person who earned it? | Beyond the gallery, where could real receipts appear in the world (on shop walls, in company lobbies, in portfolio sites) so the campaign feels like a lasting ritual and not just a moment?

title: On Me
idea: Loneliness isn't a lack of people. It's the friction of asking and the fear of being a burden. On Me turns a Mastercard payment into the invitation: send someone a specific plan, 'Thursday 6pm, noodles at Lin's, on me.' The money is pre-funded but unlocks only when you both show up and tap together. Vague 'let's catch up' becomes a real table, and the cost excuse disappears. It's for everyone, never labelled 'lonely.' Charities and employers can fund invitations for people with no one to ask. Small independent merchants join first, filling quiet hours and marking their till with a 'Regulars' tap. Priceless, made practical: money that only works when people show up for each other.
follow_up_questions: What other everyday financial moments (splitting a bill, a refund, a subscription renewal) could be redesigned to bring people together rather than to simply move money? | How could the 'only unlocks when we both show up' rule be adapted to other life situations, such as a new city, new parenthood or retirement, without changing the core mechanic? | Who is the most overlooked person who should be able to receive an On Me, and which partner could credibly send it to them?

title: Read Your Pay
idea: Your first paycheck should feel like a win, but it often arrives as a confusing document and a smaller number than you expected. Canva redesigns the payslip. A public before-and-after project shows a typical payslip turned into a clear, beautiful story of where each part of your pay went, with no advice, only clarity. Free templates let anyone make sense of their pay, and employers can brand them for a 'Day One' onboarding kit so new hires understand their first paycheck before it arrives. People share their own redesigned (dummy-data) versions with the line 'now I get it'. The same approach then extends to other intimidating documents: leases, offer letters and benefits packs. Canva makes the confusing clear.
follow_up_questions: Which other intimidating first-time documents in early adult life could Canva redesign to create a recurring platform? | How could employers and payroll providers become co-creators of the redesigned payslip, not just adopters of it? | What would make people proudly share the moment of finally understanding their pay, instead of keeping the confusion private?

title: Paid Professional
idea: Your first paycheck says you're a professional. Your first week often doesn't feel like it. Paid Professional closes that gap. Canva marks the first payday with a 'Day One Pro' kit: the first deck, one-pager, status update, email signature, and for freelancers, the first invoice and rate card. All of it is built so a beginner looks as capable as they already are. A shareable 'Day One Pro' card lets people celebrate the milestone without showing a single number. Real first-timers and their managers show the first thing they made, and employers and universities hand the kit out at onboarding. The paycheck is proof of the job. Canva helps you show it. Each new hire who adopts Canva on day one becomes a quiet champion for it inside the team.
follow_up_questions: What is the very first piece of work a new hire is judged on, and how could the brand make that moment less intimidating in your market? | How might the ritual of marking a first payday differ across cultures, and which local customs could become the campaign's most distinctive creative expressions? | Beyond templates, what product or partnership could make Canva part of a company's onboarding itself, so adoption starts on day one rather than being discovered later?

title: What It Became
idea: A first paycheck is gone in days, but everyone remembers what it turned into: the trainers, the first rent, the dinner for Mum. Canva makes that visible. A simple template lets first-time earners turn their first payday into a poster of what it became, with no amounts, just the story. Employers on Canva Teams can send a branded version to every new hire on payday, so a company's first gesture is a keepsake rather than a payslip. People share the results as #WhatItBecame, and an optional printed frame turns the best into real objects. It becomes an annual payday tradition for every new cohort, and shows Canva as the tool for marking the moments that make work feel real.
follow_up_questions: Which other 'first' moments at work (first desk, first promotion, first team you lead) could use the same 'what it became' approach? | How could employers, schools or payroll providers become distribution partners without the campaign feeling like corporate branding? | What would make people want to share their story publicly, and what would make them keep it private?

title: Regulars
idea: For many people, the most dependable human contact is being known at the corner café, barber or laundromat. Contactless payment has quietly made that contact optional. Regulars turns it back into something worth protecting. Neighbors nominate the places that make them feel known. Using only aggregated, anonymized trends, Mastercard helps identify where repeat-visit culture is fading and backs those businesses with a communal table, a weekly regulars' hour and a Regulars mark on the door. When a regular taps, a soft version of Mastercard's sonic logo becomes the sound of 'welcome back'. Local stories of regulars become the campaign. Independent researchers measure the effect on belonging. Priceless was never about what you buy. It is about being known where you buy it.
follow_up_questions: Which everyday places in your own life make you feel known, and what small ritual would protect them from disappearing? | How could the brand show its use of data for belonging in a way that visibly strengthens trust instead of triggering suspicion? | What would a 'regular' ritual look like in non-physical places, such as online communities, so the idea reaches people who can't easily leave home?

title: The Second Fitting
idea: Owners of Dior pieces often keep them untouched because they love them too much to risk changing them. The Second Fitting gives permission. Clients bring a treasured piece they no longer wear: a mother's jacket, a scuffed Saddle bag, a dress from a decade ago. A Dior atelier fits it again, repairing, reshaping or reinventing it so it can be worn. A film series follows real clients and the artisans through each appointment, from fear to the first wear. Every finished piece gets a small embroidered date and the artisan's initials inside the lining. The message: a Dior is never finished, it is only fitted to the next chapter of your life. It lives in ateliers, boutiques, social and client-submitted stories, with a limited number of appointments each season.
follow_up_questions: Which emotional moment is most powerful to film: the fear of letting the atelier touch the piece, the artisan's first cut, or the first time the client wears it again? | How could the embroidered second-fitting mark become a recognisable status symbol without turning into a gimmick, and who should be credited by name? | How can the campaign stay scarce and desirable while still inviting people with a modest, everyday Dior piece, not just the most privileged clients?

title: Paid for Making
idea: You remember your first paycheck as a number. You forget the thing you made to earn it. Paid for Making celebrates that thing: the first design anyone ever paid you for, such as a $40 logo for a cousin's bakery, a gig poster, or a wedding menu. Every story follows one rule: the amount is blurred and the work is razor sharp. Real people, and the people who paid them, show the artifact with a FIRST PAID stamp and one line on why someone said yes. The blur becomes a Canva effect anyone can use, and the stories become a living wall in the product, in out-of-home, and in social. The number fades. The work is what you keep.
follow_up_questions: What is the equivalent of the 'blur' for other moments of earned pride (first sale, first promotion, first hire), and could the campaign grow into a series? | How could the person who writes the first paycheck, such as a small business owner paying their first employee, become a second storyline for Canva's B2B audience? | What would make people share work they are proud of but not yet confident about, such as a first-time designer's imperfect poster, and how should the brand protect that vulnerability?

title: The Extra Inch
idea: Hidden inside every well-made couture garment is an extra inch of fabric, folded away so the piece can be taken in, let out and re-fitted for decades. It is the quietest promise in fashion: this was made to outlive the moment. Dior turns that secret into a campaign. Films and exhibits reveal the inch, atelier hands refit the pieces of real clients, and each mend is signed with a discreet thread mark, so repair becomes a mark of status, not a repair job. Leather goods get their own version through re-edging, re-lining and restoration. The inch also belongs to the next owner, making reuse the next chapter of the design. Luxury stops meaning new, and starts meaning room to keep going.
follow_up_questions: What other hidden, 'invisible' construction details in Dior's products could be revealed as proof of longevity, and what would they say about the house's values? | How could a signed mend become a collectable cultural object, and what would make a client proudly show it rather than conceal it? | Where is the line between a credible longevity promise and a greenwashing risk, and which proof points would the audience actually believe?

title: The Second Signature
idea: A piece of Dior is not finished when it leaves the atelier; it is finished when it has lived. The Second Signature turns repair into the most desirable mark in luxury. When an owner brings in a bag, jacket or shoe, the atelier restores it invisibly or, if the owner chooses, leaves a hand-stitched Dior mend in the house's own thread: a second signature beside the first. The campaign photographs wear like couture: a softened leather corner, a re-stitched hem, a named repairer's hands at work. Owners and ambassadors share the stories behind their marks. Launched first on a few icons such as the Saddle, Lady Dior and Bar jacket, it makes keeping a piece the ultimate statement of taste, and proves that Dior's real newness is time.
follow_up_questions: What would a 'second signature' look like and feel like so that it is unmistakably Dior yet beautiful enough that someone would request it, and not merely accept it? | Which iconic Dior pieces carry the strongest stories of being worn, loved and passed on, and who are the unexpected people, beyond celebrities, whose wear marks would make the most compelling portraits? | How could the idea reach younger, vintage-loving audiences who have never owned a new Dior piece, for example through archive finds, resale, or gifted pieces, without diluting exclusivity?

title: Keep the Tab Open
idea: Settling up is the quickest way to end a relationship: once the money is sent, there's no reason to meet. Mastercard flips that. Through partner banking and wallet apps, 'Pay me back in person' turns a split bill into an IOU measured in moments: one dinner, two coffees, a Sunday walk. Both people see the open tab, and a private nudge helps them lock a date. When it's redeemed on a Mastercard, the tab closes with a small celebratory reward. The launch film follows a 20-year-old tab between two friends who keep refusing to repay it. The platform thought: some debts are priceless. It frames loneliness as friendships quietly losing their excuses to meet, and positions Mastercard as the payments brand that understands money's social role. Pilot in a few markets, opt-in only, no public reminders.
follow_up_questions: What other 'frictionless' moments in payments (tap, one-click, auto-pay) have quietly removed a human ritual, and how could each be turned back into a reason to connect? | How could the open tab extend beyond friends to family, neighbours or former colleagues, and which relationship would make the most moving story? | What would make people proud to leave a tab open for years, and how could the 'oldest tab' become a shareable cultural symbol without creating pressure?

title: Signed, Again
idea: Dior treats repair as a second act of making. Every piece restored in a Dior atelier can be signed by the artisan who repaired it, with a discreet mark and a named entry in a repair passport that travels with the piece to its next owner. The campaign shows the hands, the benches and the owners who wear their repaired Dior with pride. A Bar jacket, a Lady Dior or a pair of shoes is no longer less perfect after repair. It has another author and a longer story. Owners choose a visible mark, a hidden one or a digital record only. Repair becomes something to show, not hide.
follow_up_questions: What would the signature look like so it feels unmistakably Dior, such as a thread color, a stitch or a stamp, and where would it sit on different products? | How could the repair passport be used by secondhand buyers and resale platforms without Dior losing control of authenticity? | Which real owner or artisan stories would be most surprising and convincing, and how could they be found without turning the campaign into a staged testimonial?

title: Payslip, Redesigned
idea: Your first paycheck is the first document that says what your work is worth, and it looks like a tax form nobody designed. 'Payslip, Redesigned' treats it as the world's most overlooked design brief. Canva reimagines the first payslip as a human document: plain-language labels, a clear 'where did my money go' view and a small moment of celebration. We release it as open templates plus a 'Your First Payslip, Explained' kit that HR teams customise in Canva with their own brand and onboarding voice. First-jobbers get an annotated version to share: 'Gross? Net? Tax code? Finally explained.' Employers become the distribution channel, showing that Canva is how companies communicate with their people, not just their customers. The platform: everything that matters in working life deserves good design, starting with the page that says you've begun.
follow_up_questions: Which other pieces of 'life paperwork' (offer letters, first leases, contracts, resignation letters) carry the same mix of emotion and confusion, and could become the next chapters of this platform? | How could employers, payroll providers or even first-jobbers co-create the redesigned payslip so it feels like a shared movement rather than a Canva stunt? | What would make a first-jobber want to share their decoded payslip publicly without feeling exposed about pay, and what mechanic protects privacy while keeping the pride?

title: Signed by Hand
idea: Dior has always been about hands. Signed by Hand turns repair from a hidden service into couture's newest signature. When a Dior piece returns to the atelier, the petite main who mends it can embroider a tiny date and initials on the repair, a scar turned into jewellery. Owners choose whether the mend is invisible, subtle or celebrated, and each piece keeps a ledger of its life: who wore it, what happened, who fixed it. The campaign films the craftspeople, not models, opens mending salons in key cities where clients bring torn hems and beloved bags, and ends with a show of mended pieces. The message: the most desirable Dior is not the newest one. It is the one with a history and a signature on it.
follow_up_questions: What other signs of a life lived, such as wear, patina or fading, could luxury treat as value to be celebrated rather than as flaws to be hidden? | How might the craftspeople become public authors, with names, voices and followings, without turning them into influencers or exposing them to pressure? | Where could this logic of a visible second chapter extend beyond clothing, for example to bags, perfume bottles or jewellery, and what would the signature look like there?

title: First Stub
idea: The first paycheck is the first proof your work has value, yet it arrives as a cryptic PDF full of codes. Canva launches First Stub: a free template kit that redesigns the pay stub into a clear one-page story. Hours worked become a visual timeline, each deduction gets a plain-language label, and a space holds a personal note from the manager. HR and team leads customise it in Canva and send it with new hires' first pay, so Canva earns a place in onboarding, not just marketing. New hires can then remix a version with the amount hidden and share it as a keepsake. The campaign shows real first-timers reading their stubs properly for the first time. Canva doesn't do payroll: the templates present information from the employer's payroll provider, so the design clarifies and never advises.
follow_up_questions: Which other 'first' documents at work (offer letter, first review, first expense report) are just as emotional and badly designed, and could become part of a wider series? | How could employers and payroll providers be brought in as partners so First Stub is built into real payroll flows rather than a separate download? | What would make a first-timer want to share their redesigned stub publicly, and how could that sharing stay privacy-safe?

title: Mended by Dior
idea: Dior turns repair into the newest status symbol. Instead of hiding wear, the atelier offers signature visible mends: a gold-thread darn on a Bar jacket, a houndstooth patch on a worn Saddle bag, a re-embroidered cannage corner. Each is signed with a discreet sewn-in mend mark recording the artisan and date, so a repaired piece becomes more personal, more collectible and more valuable than a new one. The campaign launches with a runway moment of mended icons, then invites owners everywhere to bring in their pieces, share their mend stories, and watch artists design rare 'master mends'. The message is simple and unmistakably Dior: the most elegant thing you can wear is something you have never stopped loving.
follow_up_questions: What would a visible mend look like in a category outside clothing, such as shoes, perfume bottles or jewellery, and could it become a recognisable Dior signature? | How could owners, not just the house, author their own mends so that the stories feel co-created rather than brand-controlled? | Which cultural voices (artists, tailors, craftspeople, older generations) could define what 'beautiful wear' means and challenge the idea that new equals better?

title: The Excuse
idea: Everyone has a friend who is overdue. Both want to meet, and neither wants to be the one who asks. So Mastercard becomes the excuse. Anyone can send an overdue friend a Mastercard-funded treat (a coffee, a meal, a cinema ticket at a local partner venue) that can only be redeemed together, with a note that says, in effect, 'Mastercard is making us.' The brand takes the blame, so the invitation carries no pressure. The invited friend doesn't need a Mastercard. Treats come with a deadline and a cap, and independent local venues are prioritised. No personal data is used and no one is labelled lonely. The campaign turns Priceless into a mechanism: we pay for the moment, you supply the people. Seasonal waves (new city, new job, new baby, retirement) keep it going.
follow_up_questions: Which life transitions create the biggest 'overdue' friendships, and could each become its own wave of the platform? | What is the funniest, lowest-pressure way to write the excuse so it feels human and not like a coupon? | How could the redeemed moment itself (the tap at the table) become a lasting symbol of reconnection that people share?

title: The First Invoice
idea: Everyone remembers their first paycheck. Nobody remembers the thing they made to earn it. Canva turns the first invoice into the new rite of passage. A hero film follows a teenage sticker seller, a dog walker and a career changer as they send their first, slightly embarrassing invoice, then their first polished one, and notice how clients, and they themselves, respond differently. Canva releases a collection of First Invoice templates, rate cards and thank-you notes, and invites people to share the document that got them paid, with the amount optional. The best entries become a living Museum of First Invoices, and every new earner can design a keepsake 'framed first paycheck'. The message: you don't need to feel professional first. You need to look like someone worth paying, and Canva helps you borrow that confidence until it becomes yours.
follow_up_questions: What other 'first' documents or objects in a working life (the first business card, the first pitch deck, the first 'out of office') carry as much emotion as the first invoice, and could be their own chapters? | How could the campaign celebrate people whose first paycheck came from an employer rather than a side hustle, without losing the 'first invoice' focus? | What would make a person proud, rather than exposed, to publicly share what they earned, and how might the Museum protect and honor that?

title: Tap Together
idea: Convenience took away the small human moments of daily life. Mastercard gives them back with an invitation that can't be spent alone. Anyone can send a prepaid 'On Me' treat at a local café, barbershop, cinema or noodle bar, to a friend they've drifted from, a neighbour, a colleague or a relative. It unlocks only when both people tap their cards at the same terminal, so the tap becomes a gesture of showing up together. The sender takes the social risk, and the receiver is never labelled lonely. Local merchants gain footfall, and a loneliness charity partner helps with credibility and evaluation. Piloted in a few cities, it can grow through creators, community groups and gifting moments. The money starts it. The time together is priceless.
follow_up_questions: Who is the most surprising pair of people who should be invited to tap together, and what story would that pairing tell? | Which everyday places have the strongest hidden social power in your city, and how could they become the stage for the first tap? | How could the campaign honestly address loneliness without ever naming it to the person receiving the invitation?

title: The Second Signature
idea: What if the most luxurious thing about a Dior piece was the proof it had been loved? Every repaired Dior garment or bag receives a discreet second signature from the atelier hand who restored it, so the piece carries two authors: the house and the repairer. Mending becomes the new monogram. Portraits of real owners and their well-lived pieces, shot like couture editorials with the repairer credited, launch the idea. A 'Dior Lineage' registry records each repair and owner, giving reused Dior certified provenance and higher value. Owners choose whether the mend whispers or shines, with gold thread for those who want it seen. Dior stops asking people to buy better and starts celebrating those who keep.
follow_up_questions: How loud should a repair be: should owners choose invisible, subtle or showpiece mends, and what does each choice say about status? | Which Dior pieces from the archive would make the most compelling first 'lineage' stories, and who are the unexpected owners to feature? | What service promises (lifetime repair, turnaround time, pricing) would Dior need to guarantee for the campaign to feel credible rather than cosmetic?

title: Known By Name
idea: Loneliness often hides in the smallest ritual: the café where someone is the 8:10 flat white. Payments have made that ritual silent: tap, beep, gone. Mastercard turns the beep into belonging. Cardholders opt in to share the name they like to be called with places they choose. At tap, the terminal shows it and the person behind the counter says, 'Morning, Ana.' No spend data is shared, and anyone can withdraw at any time. Small businesses receive a 'Regulars' window mark and a greeting kit. The campaign films real regulars (retirees, night-shift workers, new arrivals) and the people who know them. It extends True Name's belief that a name is identity: some things money can't buy, like being known. Start with a single neighbourhood pilot.
follow_up_questions: Which everyday places (the pharmacy, the laundromat, the bus kiosk) are the most overlooked sources of recognition, and how would the idea change in each? | How could recognition be offered to people who don't want to be noticed, so that it stays an invitation and never becomes pressure? | What would a brand have to give up or admit about its own convenience-driven products to be believable on the topic of loneliness?

title: Luck, Sewn Back
idea: Christian Dior, famously superstitious, hid a sprig of lily of the valley in the hem of his dresses for luck. We reverse the ritual: a garment's second life earns its own. Every piece mended by Dior's ateliers receives a 'lucky stitch' in muguet-white thread, hidden in the hem or worn proudly on a cuff, the owner's choice. Films follow the petites mains repairing a worn Bar jacket, a cracked Lady Dior strap, a grandmother's scarf. Pop-up Retouche salons open in Paris, Seoul and New York and, for one week, mend anything from any brand. Owners tell us why they kept it. Luxury stops promising newness and starts promising a longer story.
follow_up_questions: Which other parts of Dior's founding mythology, such as the star, the garden or the toile, could become a visual language for repair beyond the lily of the valley? | How can 'mend anything' feel like an honour rather than a giveaway, so that generosity to non-owners adds to Dior's desirability instead of diluting it? | What would make a repaired piece gain value rather than lose it, in resale, in status and in the owner's own story, and who should vouch for that?

title: Frame It: The First Paycheck Wall
idea: Everyone frames the first dollar a business earns. No one frames the first paycheck. Canva makes it a ritual. Upload or recreate your first stub, and Canva masks every sensitive detail by default, then helps you turn it into a frame-ready keepsake. Add notes like the hours it took, who you treated, or what you learned. Print it, post it, or hang it at your desk. Creators share theirs first; a public 'Paycheck Wall' collects stories without ever showing amounts. Employers can gift a First Stub Frame kit at onboarding, bringing Canva into the team on day one. The message: you didn't just get paid, you became someone who works. Make it worth framing.
follow_up_questions: How could the ritual spread beyond the first job, to first promotions, first freelance invoices or first business sales, without losing the emotional power of 'the first'? | What would make parents, mentors or managers want to take part, and what role could they play in the ritual? | Where could a physical moment (a printed frame, a poster in a workplace, a pop-up on payday) amplify a mostly digital campaign?

title: Dior Mended
idea: Dior turns repair into the new status symbol. Clients bring any Dior piece, however worn, to the atelier, where the petites mains mend it with a signature stitch drawn from Dior's codes (cannage, toile de Jouy, the bee) or, if preferred, invisibly. Every mend is signed and dated by its artisan. The campaign portrays owners and artisans together, telling the story behind each tear: the dance, the dash for a taxi, the daughter who borrowed it. A scuffed Lady Dior or a darned Bar jacket becomes proof of a life fully lived, and the mend becomes the most desirable detail in the wardrobe. Launch with films and portraits, boutique repair salons and a small exhibition of mended icons, then scale city by city.
follow_up_questions: What would make a mend something people want to be seen with, and how can a repair become collectable rather than just functional? | Which other Dior codes, rituals or craft moments could carry the repair story to audiences who would never visit an atelier? | How might the platform expand over time into lineage, passing pieces on, and long-term care without losing the simple power of the mend?

title: Seat for Two
idea: Loneliness rarely needs more opportunities. It needs an easier way to ask. Seat for Two gives every Mastercard cardholder at partner cafes, restaurants and venues a ready-made invitation: a card with a pre-paid second seat on Mastercard. Hand it to a neighbour, an old friend you've lost touch with, or a coworker you only know by Slack. The awkward question of who pays disappears, leaving only 'want to come?' Partner venues also host open tables where invitations can be shared with new faces. Mastercard turns Priceless into a practical gesture: the best thing money can buy is a reason to say yes. Start with a pilot in a few cities, track redeemed seats and repeat meetups, and let the stories spread.
follow_up_questions: Which relationship is easiest to invite, and which is most meaningful: a neighbour, a lapsed friend or a colleague? How would that change who the campaign speaks to? | What would make receiving an invitation feel like a gift rather than pity, and how should the card look and sound to achieve that? | How could a one-time invitation turn into a standing habit, and should the brand help with that second step or leave it to the people involved?

title: The Second Fitting
idea: Every Dior couture piece begins with a fitting. We extend that ritual across the life of the garment. Owners bring any Dior piece, from a Bar jacket to a Lady Dior, back to the atelier for a Second Fitting: restored, reshaped for who they are now, or prepared for its next wearer. The artisan signs the work with a small stitched label, and mends can be invisible or proudly visible. The campaign follows pieces through decades of fittings, showing hands, scars and new lives, and makes the case that a Dior piece is never finished, only continued. Status shifts from owning the newest piece to being known by the atelier. Launch with the service open in flagship cities, then tell the stories it creates.
follow_up_questions: What would make a visibly repaired Dior piece a status symbol rather than a sign of wear, and who would need to wear it first for that to be believed? | How could the Second Fitting work for customers who bought pre-owned or vintage Dior, and would welcoming them strengthen or dilute the House's relationship with its clients? | Which atelier artisans should become the faces of the campaign, and how might their craft be shown to feel intimate rather than corporate?

title: The Mend Is the Signature
idea: Dior turns the mend into its newest signature. Clients bring in a torn Bar jacket, a scuffed Lady Dior or a snagged silk scarf, and the petites mains answer by embroidering the damage rather than hiding it: cannage stitching, pearls along a tear, a gilded star-shaped patch. Each mend is designed with the owner, signed by the artisan and recorded on the piece's inner label, so a repaired Dior becomes more valuable, not less. Purists can choose an invisible mend. The campaign films these conversations as intimate portraits of a story, a scar and a needle. It launches with a live atelier window on Avenue Montaigne, then continues as a permanent, tiered service. The message: Dior isn't kept pristine. It's kept.
follow_up_questions: What other moments of wear or loss, beyond a tear, could the House honour as the start of a piece's next chapter? | How might the mend travel beyond the atelier, for example into the collections, the runway or a client's own hands, without becoming a trend that cheapens it? | Who besides the owner should be part of a mend's story, such as the artisan, the previous owner or the next one, and how would that change what is shown and shared?

title: The Covered Invite
idea: Lonely people rarely lack company so much as the nerve to ask for it. Inviting feels like imposing, and accepting feels like a cost. The Covered Invite removes both. Any Mastercard holder can send a simple digital invite to a coffee, a meal or a class at a participating independent venue. The invite carries one line: 'It's covered. Just come.' Mastercard pays for the guest's first item, who doesn't need a Mastercard, and either side can say 'maybe later' with no awkwardness. Merchants fill quiet hours, and the brand shows what Priceless means in practice: money clears the way so the moment itself can be priceless. Themed waves such as new neighbours, old friends and the first week back can keep the platform running through the year.
follow_up_questions: Which moments of life change (moving, a new baby, retirement, remote work) are the most powerful and least served entry points for an invitation? | How could the invitation itself become a cultural object that people want to share, keep or answer, rather than a voucher? | What would make a local merchant feel like a host in this idea rather than a redemption point?

title: Your First Paycheck, Finally Readable
idea: The first paycheck is one of the proudest moments of working life, yet the payslip that comes with it looks like a tax form. Canva fixes it. We launch a set of free visual payslip templates that lead with what you earned and then show, in plain words, where the rest went. Nothing is uploaded and no advice is given; the templates simply make the information clear. Employers and payroll teams get a 'First Paycheck Welcome Kit' to send with a new hire's first pay. Individuals can also make a 'Share the win' card that hides the numbers and shows only 'My first paycheck'. The campaign shows Canva's core skill, making complicated things clear, on a document everyone has received and nobody has enjoyed, and it opens the door to other first-job documents.
follow_up_questions: Which other first-job documents (offer letters, contracts, benefits guides) are just as confusing, and which would make the strongest next chapter? | How could payroll providers or HR platforms work with Canva so the readable payslip arrives automatically with the first pay? | What would make someone proud to share a payslip card, and how can the campaign keep the amount private while keeping the moment public?

title: Day One, Looking Like You Belong
idea: The first paycheck is proof you belong, yet most people spend their first weeks feeling like they're faking it. Canva launches the First Paycheck Kit: templates for the things new workers are suddenly asked to make, such as a team intro slide, a 30-60-90 day plan, a weekly update, a freelance invoice and a refreshed CV. The campaign is told through real first-jobbers confessing the small thing they secretly didn't know how to make, and how it turned out fine. Payday unlocks a one-tap thank-you card to share with whoever helped you get there, with no amounts shown. Employers and universities can hand the kit to new hires, turning a personal confidence boost into a habit that follows people into their teams.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job moment (the intro slide, the first invoice, the first update to a boss) is the most universally nerve-racking, and could it become the single hero story of the campaign? | How could the kit work for people whose first paycheck looks very different, such as gig workers, apprentices, family business staff or people in markets with other pay rhythms? | What would make an employer proudly share the kit with every new hire, and how would Canva know that this habit is carrying into team use?

title: Two-Tap: The Card That Only Works With Company
idea: Loneliness often lasts because the first invitation feels awkward. Two-Tap is a Mastercard gift card that only works when two people tap it together. You are not giving money, you are giving a plan that cannot be spent alone. Friends and family can send one without saying 'you seem lonely'. An 'Open Pair' option matches a card with a companion through libraries, charities and local clubs, so no one is left out. Launch in one or two cities with cafés, cinemas, classes and community venues, and measure how many pairs redeem the card and make a second plan. Priceless has always been about moments that money cannot buy. Two-Tap makes the payment itself ask for one.
follow_up_questions: Which everyday places (a laundromat, a barbershop, a park kiosk) could offer a Two-Tap plan that feels natural and not staged? | How could the pairing be designed so that being matched with a stranger feels safe and easy, not like a social test? | What would a second and third plan look like, so that one invitation grows into a lasting habit of meeting up?

title: The New Look, Again
idea: In 1947, Dior changed fashion by reshaping what already existed. Today, the ateliers do it again. Each season, clients bring in a piece they love, such as a worn Bar jacket, a scuffed Lady Dior or an inherited coat, and the petites mains repair, re-cut and reimagine it into the season's silhouette. The best transformations walk in a runway moment and star in a film series, each told through its owner's memory and the artisan who remade it. The service stays open year-round, with some places offered by public draw. Repair stops being what you do when something breaks and becomes what you do when you love something too much to let it end. A discreet star stitched inside marks every piece reborn.
follow_up_questions: What is the one piece in your own wardrobe you would never part with, and what would you want a master artisan to change about it? | How could scarcity, such as limited atelier slots, be used as a feature of the campaign without making the idea feel closed or elitist? | Which other brand icons or founder moments contain an act of reinvention that could turn repair and reuse into a heritage-led story?

title: The Dior Mend
idea: Dior turns repair into the rarest thing the house can give: a mark that can't be bought, only earned. The atelier creates a signature mend, a fine stitch in a Dior-grey thread with a small numbered label, applied to pieces that have lived, been loved and been restored by the petites mains. Owners can choose an invisible repair or a signed one. Each returns with a handwritten note from the atelier hand that worked on it. The campaign films the hands, not the models, and the stories of people who kept their pieces: a Bar jacket worn for decades, a Lady Dior passed down. Pop-up Mending Salons open in a few cities with limited capacity, and a runway moment shows mended pieces as the newest detail in couture. Time becomes the house's finest finish.
follow_up_questions: What would make a mend mark desirable enough that someone would proudly show it off, and where on a garment or bag should it live? | Which pieces and owner stories in Dior's history, or in clients' wardrobes, would make the most moving first chapter of this campaign? | How could the idea extend beyond Dior's own products, for instance to a client's much-loved non-Dior item, without losing exclusivity or craft integrity?

title: Pay Together
idea: Loneliness lives in the gap between 'we should catch up' and actually asking. Pay Together closes it with money that only works in company. Someone sends a small 'Together' gift, say a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles, as a virtual Mastercard. It unlocks only when both people's phones are at the same local independent venue. The payment is the invitation, so nobody has to awkwardly ask. For people with no one to send it to, Open Tap pairs them with neighbours through befriending charities and community groups, in public places. Gifts are small, spend isn't the goal, and no one's data is used to find lonely people. Success is counted in meetings made, not money moved. Priceless, made literal: it's worth nothing until it's shared.
follow_up_questions: Who is the first person you would send a Together gift to, and what would make you hesitate? What does that reveal about the real barrier to reaching out? | Which local places in your own neighbourhood already work as third places, and how would a Together gift change what happens there? | Beyond coffee, what other everyday payments (a bus fare, a gym class, a cinema ticket, a parking space) could be redesigned so they only work in company, and which would be the most surprising?

title: Frame the First One
idea: Direct deposit killed the first paycheck as an object. Nobody frames a bank notification. Canva brings the ritual back. 'Frame the First One' is a free Canva toolkit that turns a first-pay moment into a keepsake. Upload or type it, the amount is auto-hidden, and you design the story around it: the job, the date and what it became (a rent deposit, dinner for mum, a pair of shoes). Frames can be shared, printed through Canva Print, or hung in a growing Museum of First Paychecks, seeded with real framed checks from parents, grandparents and public figures. Employers can gift a branded starter frame at onboarding through Canva for Teams. The truth at the centre: your first pay isn't about the money, it's proof that someone valued what you made, and Canva helps you make that visible.
follow_up_questions: Which other work milestones have lost their physical ritual (first desk, last day, a promotion) and could Canva own a series of 'objects for moments' rather than one? | What would make the Museum of First Paychecks feel like a cultural institution people want to visit and contribute to, rather than a template gallery? | How might the idea work in markets where first pay is cash, mobile money or informal, and what local rituals could it build on?

title: The Number You Didn't Design
idea: Your first paycheck is the first number someone else designed for you. Canva helps you design the next conversation. Launch with a ritual: creators take their real first payslip (amounts blurred) and redraw it as a Worth Deck, turning each line into a slide on impact, growth and what's next. Canva releases the Worth Deck kit: impact timeline, wins one-pager, learning plan and the ask. A companion 'Receive it well' kit gives managers templates for review and growth conversations, so the idea works for teams, not against them. Run it at first-job and graduation moments through creators, campuses and LinkedIn. The message: visual communication is a career skill, and Canva is where it's built. It is not about demanding more, but about making your value impossible to overlook.
follow_up_questions: What other 'numbers someone else designed for us' (grades, ratings, follower counts, job titles) could Canva help people respond to visually? | How could managers and HR teams become co-authors of the campaign rather than its audience, so it builds adoption inside companies? | What would a Worth Deck look like in cultures where negotiating pay is taboo, and how should the idea change there?

title: Two-Tap Treat
idea: Reaching out feels like an imposition, so we give people a reason. Two-Tap Treat lets you send a friend, relative or someone you've lost touch with a small treat at a local café, bakery or cinema. The catch: it only unlocks when both of you tap at the same place, at the same time. Money that only works together. Mastercard turns the act of paying into the act of meeting, using tap technology and its local merchant network. Unclaimed treats flow into a community pool that funds free tables for strangers, so no gift is ever wasted. It is opt-in, privacy-first and never labels anyone as lonely. It starts in neighbourhood cafés with paired physical cards, then scales to family gifting, workplaces and seasonal moments. Priceless, made practical.
follow_up_questions: What other everyday payment moments (splitting a bill, a tip, a round of drinks, a subscription) could be redesigned so they require, or reward, doing something together? | How could the 'only works together' mechanic be adapted for people who cannot easily meet in person, such as long-distance family or housebound older adults, without losing the sense of shared presence? | Which local merchants or community spaces would benefit most from a connection-driving footfall boost, and what would they need from the brand to take part beyond discounts?

title: The Second Signature
idea: Dior turns repair into the house's most intimate signature. Any authentic Dior piece, including pre-owned or inherited, can be mended at the atelier. The owner may choose to cover the repair with a small embroidery from Christian Dior's lucky codes: a star, lily of the valley, wheat ear. Inside the lining, the artisan stitches their initials and the date. Each mark records another life, so the most loved pieces become the most prized. The campaign films real owners alongside the petites mains, then invites people to show their mark: 'Ask to see the second signature.' It starts as a pilot on the Bar jacket and Lady Dior, with real repair numbers and turnaround times published so the promise stays credible.
follow_up_questions: What would make a visible repair mark feel like a status symbol to a client rather than evidence of damage, and who should be the first people seen wearing it? | How could the mark system grow beyond the lucky codes, for example by letting clients co-design a mark, without losing the exclusivity and craft of the atelier? | Which proof points (turnaround time, repair volumes, artisan credits) would make a sceptical luxury client believe the promise, and how can they be shared without sounding like a sustainability report?

title: Lucky Thread
idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into hems for luck, and the house still honours his superstition. Lucky Thread makes that ritual the reward for keeping a Dior alive. Whenever a piece returns to the atelier for repair or restyling, the artisan finishes it with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining. The mark can't be bought, only earned through years of wear. Repair moves from the back room to the front of the boutique, with the mending artisan named on the ticket. The campaign shows well-loved Dior, such as frayed cuffs, re-soled heels and re-lined Bar jackets, as the most desirable luxury: proof of a life lived. Marked pieces carry a certificate that follows them into resale, so each mend adds value and the next owner inherits the luck. New luxury says 'own me.' Dior says 'keep me.'
follow_up_questions: What would be the most surprising, emotionally charged place or person to feature the first muguet-marked piece, and who deserves to tell its story? | How could the mark grow into a collector culture, such as the most-mended piece or the oldest piece in service, without encouraging damage for its own sake? | Which other Dior rituals or superstitions, such as the lucky star or the house's grey, could carry other parts of the reuse journey like gifting, inheriting or lending?

title: Pay Day One: Give the First Paycheck the Design It Deserves
idea: The first paycheck is one of life's proudest moments, yet it arrives as an invisible deposit and a payslip no one can read. Canva fixes the design. 'Pay Day One' is a free kit for employers: a personal first-payday card from the manager, plus a plain-visual explainer showing what gross means, where each slice went and what reached the bank. Then comes 'Frame the First One', a public invitation to design a keepsake of your first paycheck with the number hidden and only the meaning visible: what it bought, who you called, how it felt. Print it, frame it, share it. HR gets a better first month, newcomers get a ritual, and Canva proves that design makes work feel human.
follow_up_questions: Which other overlooked 'first' moments at work (first invoice, first promotion, first team you lead) are delivered through dull documents that Canva could turn into rituals? | How could the campaign honor very different first earnings, such as a teen's cash job, a gig payment or a freelancer's first client, without implying one 'right' career start? | Who is best placed to carry this into real workplaces (payroll platforms, HR tools, schools, first-job employers), and what would make them want to co-own it?

title: Known at the Tap
idea: Contactless made paying faster and quietly removed the small hellos that make a neighbourhood feel like yours. Mastercard fixes the one thing it controls: the tap. Cardholders opt in to share a chosen first name with independent cafés, shops and barbers that join the pilot. When they tap, the terminal shows 'Morning, Dana', so staff can greet them like a regular. No purchase history is shared, and the name appears only at that merchant. Research on weak ties shows that the barista who knows your order lifts wellbeing. The campaign tells real stories from participating shops, celebrates a 'Regular of the Year' in each neighbourhood, and gives merchants a Priceless Regulars sticker for the window. The most repeated moment in payments becomes the smallest daily proof that someone sees you.
follow_up_questions: How could the idea work for people who are not regulars anywhere yet, such as new arrivals in a city, without making them feel singled out? | What other small, repeated moments in payments or banking could be redesigned to add a human touch, and which of them would people welcome rather than find intrusive? | How would you measure whether a greeting at the till actually changes how connected people feel, and what would count as proof that the campaign is working?

title: The Slow Lane
idea: Mastercard helped make paying instant. A side effect: for many people, the checkout chat is the only conversation of the day. So Mastercard confesses: 'We made paying faster. Not everything should be.' In partner grocers, pharmacies and markets, one lane becomes The Slow Lane, open to everyone, with a simple sign: 'This lane takes its time.' Cashiers opt in and are recognised and given the time to talk. An optional 'Slow Tap' terminal mode replaces the efficient beep with a warmer pause. The launch film is the confession, and the campaign grows through city Slow Hours, cashier 'hosts' and a sonic signature for slowness. No data targeting, no labels, just a small, visible permission to be human at the till.
follow_up_questions: Where else has Mastercard's drive for speed removed small human moments (tolls, transit, delivery, online checkout), and could each become its own 'slow' space? | How could cashiers and local merchants co-own the idea so that it feels like their tradition and not a brand programme? | What would make the Slow Lane feel inviting for someone who is shy or reluctant to talk, and how can it let people choose the level of interaction?
